statement: Strehl ratio S = I_peak(actual PSF) / I_peak(diffraction-limited PSF, same aperture/wavelength/no aberration).
source: Strehl (1902); standard definition, e.g. Born & Wolf, Principles of Optics.
fidelity: exact -- universally agreed definition, no free parameters.

statement: Strehl ratio S >= 0.8 (Marechal criterion) is the conventional threshold for 'diffraction-limited' performance, corresponding to an RMS wavefront error below ~lambda/14.
source: Marechal (1947); summarized in ResearchGate: 'Marechal condition and the effect of aberrations on Strehl intensity', and 'Understanding Strehl Ratio in Optical Systems' (Optics for Hire).
fidelity: exact -- this is the standard, widely-cited numerical threshold.

statement: For small wavefront errors, S ~= exp(-sigma^2), sigma = RMS wavefront error in radians.
source: Marechal (1947) approximation, as commonly used in astronomical optics (see ResearchGate: 'Limitations and applicability of the Marechal approximation').
fidelity: approximate by construction (valid for sigma up to ~2 rad per the source) -- used here only for order-of-magnitude error-budget estimates, not as a precision correction.

statement: MTF(fx,fy) = |FFT2D(PSF)(fx,fy)| / |FFT2D(PSF)(0,0)|, radially averaged to MTF(f). MTF50/MTF10 are the frequencies where MTF(f)=0.5 / 0.1.
source: Standard Fourier optics; e.g. Goodman, Introduction to Fourier Optics.

statement: Airy diffraction-limited first-null diameter = 2 x 1.22 x lambda x v_r / a_hole for a circular aperture.
F/# = v_r / a_hole (image-space f-number for a single circular aperture acting as the system stop).
RMS spot radius = sqrt( sum(I * r^2) / sum(I) ), the second-moment / rms radius of the intensity distribution.
source: Standard optical metric; already implemented as stage1_v2/physics.py::second_moment_radius, reused here rather than reimplemented.

statement: Optical throughput (power fraction admitted by a single sub-aperture relative to the full natural pupil) = (a_hole / D_pupil)^2.
source: Energy conservation for a uniformly-illuminated circular aperture; generalizes the project's own earlier photometry formula T = N*(pi*a_hole^2/4)/A_total (IYPT_Pinhole_Master_Formulas_and_Pipeline.md Sec 2.11) to a single hole (N=1).

statement: Retinal illuminance (Td) = scene luminance (cd/m^2) x entrance pupil area (mm^2). 1 Td = the retinal illuminance from a 1 cd/m^2 surface through a 1 mm^2 pupil.
source: Troland (1916, as 'photon'; renamed troland later); Wikipedia 'Troland', Illuminating Engineering Society 'troland' definition.
fidelity: exact -- standard photometric unit definition. Does not correct for the Stiles-Crawford effect (see stiles_crawford entry).

statement: CIE standard photopic luminous efficacy = 683 lm/W at 555 nm, used to convert between radiometric (W) and photometric (lm/cd) units.
source: CIE 1924 photopic luminosity function, international standard.
fidelity: exact at 555nm; the project's other tested wavelengths (450/650nm) use the standard V(lambda) photopic curve, which is NOT flat -- see photometry.py for how this is applied.

statement: Human photopic contrast sensitivity function (CSF) is band-pass, peaking around 4 cycles/degree, dropping off at both lower and higher spatial frequencies; foveal cutoff (CSF->1, i.e. contrast threshold ~100%) around 50-60 cpd.
source: NCBI Bookshelf 'Contrast Sensitivity Function' overview; multiple reviews cite the ~4 cpd photopic peak (some report 2-5 cpd, others 5-8 cpd for related tasks).
fidelity: approximate -- this project implements a SIMPLIFIED parametric band-pass curve matched to the PEAK LOCATION (~4 cpd) and general shape reported in the literature, NOT the full multi-parameter Barten (1999) CSF model, which requires additional physiological parameters beyond what a literature search alone can safely reproduce. Labeled 'heuristic_csf' wherever used -- see contrast.py.

statement: Alternative CSF parametrization (Mannos & Sakrison) peaking at ~8 cycles/degree, normalized to a maximum of 1 -- used in image compression/coding literature.
source: Mannos & Sakrison, as summarized in 'Contrast sensitivity vs spatial frequency -- the last word' (kasson.com) and related CSF reviews.
fidelity: approximate -- offered as a second CSF variant per the brief's request to implement multiple accepted models where more than one exists; peak location differs from the 4 cpd photopic figure above, reflecting genuine variation across published CSF studies.

statement: In the mesopic/low-light (DeVries-Rose) regime, contrast sensitivity (and detection SNR) scales as sqrt(retinal illuminance); in the photopic (Weber) regime, contrast threshold is approximately constant (independent of illuminance).
source: Rose (1946, 1948); DeVries; summarized in 'Mechanisms and Meaning of DeVries-Rose Adaptation' (Donner & Fagerholm, 1996) and 'The Rose model, revisited' (JOSA A, 1999).
fidelity: the SCALING LAW (SNR ~ sqrt(flux)) is reproduced exactly per Rose's original photon-counting argument (first-principles Poisson statistics); the specific luminance thresholds separating scotopic/mesopic/photopic regimes are approximate, standard textbook values, not re-derived from Rose's original data.

source: Standard definition; e.g. schorsch.com 'Contrast' glossary, IES 'luminance contrast'.

statement: Blackwell (1946) measured contrast-detection thresholds (50% detection probability) as a function of target angular size and background luminance from ~90,000 observations -- the classical reference dataset for human contrast-threshold vs. luminance, still used in lighting/visibility engineering.
source: Blackwell, H.R. (1946), 'Contrast Thresholds of the Human Eye'; summarized in arXiv:1405.4209 ('Human Contrast Threshold and Astronomical Visibility').
fidelity: cited for context only -- Blackwell's task (detecting a uniform circular target against a uniform background) differs from this project's task (resolving a retinal PSF/optotype), so this project does NOT claim to apply Blackwell's specific threshold curves quantitatively; it is referenced as the well-established anchor for 'visual contrast threshold literature exists and looks like this', per the brief's request to document it.

statement: 20/20 (normal) visual acuity corresponds to a minimum angle of resolution (MAR) of 1 arcmin, equivalent to resolving ~30 cycles/degree; foveal photoreceptor (Nyquist) sampling limit is ~60 cpd. At 30 cpd, the eye's own optical MTF is reported as ~0.4 for a 2mm pupil, dropping to ~0.16 for a 5.8mm pupil.
source: Norman Koren, 'Understanding resolution and MTF'; StatPearls 'Contrast Sensitivity'.
fidelity: the MAR<->cpd conversion is an exact geometric identity (2 arcmin per cycle => 30 cpd at 1 arcmin MAR); the specific MTF values (0.4 at 2mm, 0.16 at 5.8mm pupil) are reported figures used here ONLY as external validation reference points, not re-derived.

statement: Visual Strehl ratio in the Spatial domain (VSX): the eye's PSF and the diffraction-limited PSF (same pupil) are each weighted by a neural weighting function (the inverse Fourier transform of the neural contrast sensitivity function), and VSX is the ratio of the two weighted-PSF peak values. Shown to correlate with subjective best focus and visual performance.
source: Thibos, Hong, Bradley, Cheng (2004), 'Statistical variation of aberration structure...' and follow-on work; summarized in 'Computational Aspects of the Visual Strehl Ratio' (ResearchGate) and 'Normative best-corrected values of the visual image quality metric VSX...' (PubMed).
fidelity: CONCEPT reproduced (PSF vs diffraction-limited PSF, both neurally weighted); this project's neural weighting function uses the SIMPLIFIED heuristic CSF model above (csf_photopic_peak), not Thibos et al.'s validated interferometric neural CSF -- labeled 'vsx_approx' everywhere it is computed, and should not be treated as a bit-exact reproduction of the clinical VSX metric.

statement: Light entering the pupil off-axis (near the pupil margin) is less effective at stimulating photoreceptors than light entering near the pupil center (the Stiles-Crawford effect of the first kind) -- apodizes the effective pupil, somewhat suppressing the contribution of a large natural pupil's edge relative to a small, centered pinhole.
fidelity: NOT numerically modeled in this project (optional per the brief) -- noted qualitatively in the error budget only, since it would require an additional apodization parameter this project has not sourced a specific numerical model for.

statement: Typical (non-pinhole-corrected) human eye higher-order aberration RMS wavefront error is ~0.33-0.38 micron over a naturally dilated 6mm pupil in healthy young adults; this shrinks sharply for smaller (or artificially stopped-down) pupils since higher-order Zernike terms scale steeply with aperture radius.
source: Multiple studies summarized via ScienceDirect/PMC reviews of ocular wavefront aberrometry (e.g. mean HOA RMS 0.334 +/- 0.192 micron across labs; ~0.38 micron over 6mm pupil, ages 18-40).
fidelity: the 6mm-pupil figure is a directly reported literature value; the claim that it 'shrinks sharply' for a pinhole-scale aperture is a qualitative, well-established optical fact (aberration scaling with aperture) applied here for the error budget, not a specific re-derived numerical scaling law for THIS eye model.
